video_title: Cambria Global EW 3 ETF and 351 ETF Conversions (GEX) | Meb Faber
gist: In a Cambria webinar and Q&A, Meb Faber pitches the November launch of GEX, a 25-basis-point global non-market-cap-weighted equity ETF seeded through a Section 351 tax-deferred exchange, arguing that a US CAPE near 42 and an all-time-low 1.04% S&P dividend yield make concentrated market-cap US exposure a yellow-light setup. He details the mechanical rules and custodian frictions of 351 conversions, defends shareholder yield over dividend and dividend-growth strategies as a net-of-buyback problem, and says rates could and should go higher because fixed income offers too little spread over T-bills.

insights.claim: Meb Faber says the US Shiller CAPE ratio sits around 42 and is roughly one week of rallies from eclipsing the 1999 all-time high of about 44, which he says pushes the market into bubble territory rather than merely expensive.
insights.speaker: Meb Faber
insights.so_what: A CAPE at the dot-com peak argues for trimming US market-cap beta and funding the trim with cheaper foreign, value and small-cap exposure — though Faber stresses there is no ceiling on valuation and it could run to 50 or 60 as Japan's did.
insights.quote: Remember the US is 42 today

insights.claim: Faber states that no country in his dataset has ever closed a year at a CAPE ratio of 40 and gone on to deliver above-average subsequent 10-year real returns — a batting average of zero.
insights.speaker: Meb Faber
insights.so_what: Frames current US valuations as a hard constraint on the next decade of real returns, supporting lower forward-return assumptions and higher non-US allocations.
insights.quote: never once in history have we found a market that closed a year, a country, at a CAPE ratio of 40 and had above average 10-year real returns

insights.claim: Foreign stocks and value have outperformed for two straight years — up roughly 30% last year and another 25% this year per Faber — yet he says clients and advisors will ignore it until the S&P stops delivering 15%.
insights.speaker: Meb Faber
insights.so_what: A two-year relative-strength move in diversifiers that is still being ignored suggests flows into ex-US and value have substantial room to run once US returns flatten.
insights.quote: they're definitely creaming the S&P, but no one really cares if the S&P is still doing 15%

insights.claim: Faber argues market-cap weighting is structurally a buy-high-sell-low mechanism that concentrates capital in whatever has already risen most and is therefore most expensive, citing Rob Arnott's framing.
insights.speaker: Meb Faber
insights.so_what: The core intellectual case for non-market-cap-weighted global equity products and for questioning ACWI or SPY as default core holdings.
insights.quote: he talks about market cap weighting and he says the problem, you know, is is they buy high and sell low, and we definitely are feeling that today

insights.claim: The two binding rules of a 351 ETF exchange are that no single contributed position may exceed 25% and the top five may not exceed 50%, requiring roughly 11 or 12 distinct holdings — though contributed ETFs are looked through to their underlying stocks, so SPY can be paired with one concentrated name.
insights.speaker: Meb Faber
insights.so_what: The ETF pass-through is the practical workaround that makes conversions feasible for holders of a single dominant stock; advisors can pre-screen eligibility in their head.
insights.quote: First stock can't be over 25, top five over 50.

insights.claim: Only liquid publicly listed stocks and ETFs qualify for Cambria's 351 contributions — microcap junior miners, foreign stocks into a US fund, hedge and mutual fund interests, derivatives, options, futures, leveraged ETFs, covered-call ETFs and Dogecoin are all rejected, and the contributed book must roughly match the launching fund's prospectus.
insights.speaker: Meb Faber
insights.so_what: Sets the eligibility boundary advisors must screen against before pitching a client on a conversion.

insights.claim: Faber insists a 351 conversion is tax deferral, not a tax dodge — basis carries over so the eventual liability will likely be larger as the fund compounds — and says the financial media consistently gets this wrong.
insights.speaker: Meb Faber
insights.so_what: Reframes the product for compliance conversations and undercuts the headline risk that a crackdown would kill the structure.
insights.quote: No, to be clear, most likely these funds will grow, they will compound, and the tax liability will actually be bigger. It's just delayed

insights.claim: Faber says the Treasury has recently been examining 351s and long-short structures and he actively welcomes it, because rule clarification would open the structure at wirehouses like Merrill and Morgan and eliminate bad actors who launch a portfolio and turn it over on day one.
insights.speaker: Meb Faber
insights.so_what: Regulatory clarity is the gating catalyst for 351 conversions scaling into mainstream wirehouse distribution — a perceived headline risk Faber reads as an upside catalyst.
insights.quote: I hope to God they take a look at 351s and clarify the rules because I think that clears the deck on making them available everywhere, Merrill and Morgan and on and on.

insights.claim: Custodian support is the main bottleneck for 351 conversions: Schwab runs a dedicated 351 department, Fidelity refuses outright, and wirehouse clients generally cannot participate unless assets are held away — with Faber predicting Fidelity will eventually offer its own version while blocking outside providers.
insights.speaker: Meb Faber
insights.so_what: Custodian choice is now a competitive variable for RIAs — Faber reports billion-dollar RIAs leaving Fidelity partly over this and its $100 ETF fee — and implies a closing window before large custodians vertically integrate the product.
insights.quote: Schwab loves it. They whole 351 department. Fidelity won't do it.

insights.claim: Faber estimates roughly $20 billion of 351 ETF exchanges have been completed to date, sees hundreds of billions up for grabs over the next couple of years, and identifies held-away concentrated stock — such as a client with $75 million in Home Depot outside the advisory relationship — as the single largest untapped pool.
insights.speaker: Meb Faber
insights.so_what: Quantifies the addressable market and gives independent RIAs a concrete business-development wedge: converting held-away concentrated positions brings previously unbillable assets under the fee umbrella.
insights.quote: I think there's hundreds and hundreds of billions up for grabs in the next um next couple years

insights.claim: Faber argues concentrated single-stock positions are on average a terrible idea regardless of survivorship-biased success stories, invoking Enron and CMGI against the Nvidia and Berkshire winners investors cite.
insights.speaker: Meb Faber
insights.so_what: The demand-side rationale for the whole 351 conversion business, and the research angle advisors should lead with when approaching founders, VCs and public-company C-suites who Faber says are almost entirely unaware the structure exists.
insights.quote: concentrated positions on average are a horrible, terrible very bad idea

insights.claim: Cambria is launching its global equal-weight ETF under the ticker GEX in mid-November via a 351 seeding, with contributions needing to be arranged within about the next month and all major work done by late September or early October.
insights.speaker: Meb Faber
insights.so_what: A hard, dated window for converting concentrated stock into diversified global equity without triggering capital gains this year.

insights.claim: GEX will charge a 25 basis point management fee as its only fee — below ACWI — and will hold roughly the top 500 market-cap companies across the ~45 to 50 investable developed and emerging countries, explicitly a global fund rather than an ex-US one like EFA.
insights.speaker: Meb Faber
insights.so_what: Positions GEX as one of the cheapest non-market-cap-weighted global equity ETFs available, with roughly half to two-thirds US weight by global market cap.
insights.quote: 25 basis points, you know, very few global equity ETFs are that low, particularly the ones that are not market cap weighted. That's less than ACWI

insights.claim: Faber thinks low-cost global non-market-cap-weighted equity could become a $50 billion category and would not be surprised if the 351-seeded funds became Cambria's largest within two years, with the firm open to custom conversions for advisors bringing roughly $500 million.
insights.speaker: Meb Faber
insights.so_what: Sizes the sponsor's ambition and reveals a negotiable pipeline — large allocators can effectively commission a bespoke tax-deferred vehicle outside the spring/fall cadence.
insights.quote: If you told me in 2 years that these are our largest funds, uh I wouldn't be I wouldn't necessarily be surprised.

themes.theme: Shareholder Yield vs the Dividend Complex

insights.claim: Faber argues that for a taxable investor focused on compounding, dividends are actively harmful because they force a taxable distribution that must then be reinvested — the basis for Cambria's TAX fund targeting low-to-no dividend yield stocks, which he thinks is eventually a $100 billion concept with no competitors.
insights.speaker: Meb Faber
insights.so_what: Implies high-dividend funds carry a persistent after-tax drag; Faber notes the edge is small versus the S&P today at an all-time-low 1.04% dividend yield but large versus dedicated high-dividend strategies.
insights.quote: if you're a taxable investor whose focus is compounding, the last thing in the world you want is dividends

insights.claim: Faber says the average US stock is a net share issuer, so gross buyback announcements mislead — a company announcing a 5% buyback while granting 7% a year in stock-based compensation has a negative net buyback yield.
insights.speaker: Meb Faber
insights.so_what: Screening on net shareholder yield rather than gross buybacks or dividend yield is the operative edge; dilution is the hidden negative carry inside most dividend strategies.
insights.quote: Average stock in the US is a issuer. It means you're getting diluted.

insights.claim: Cambria's three original shareholder yield ETFs — SYLD, FYLD and EYLD — have all now reached 10-year track records and rank top decile, in some cases top 5%, versus their categories while remaining cap-size, sector and country agnostic subject to one-third caps.
insights.speaker: Meb Faber
insights.so_what: Provides the live out-of-sample evidence for buyback-inclusive yield beating dividend-only screens, now with a decade of history.

insights.claim: Faber contends the dividend-growth chart every asset manager publishes rests on a faulty study, and that properly screened, dividend growth delivers roughly market-like returns while dividend yield is the better strategy.
insights.speaker: Meb Faber
insights.so_what: Directly challenges the marketing foundation of a large ETF category; if correct, dividend-growth funds charge a narrative premium for market returns.

insights.claim: Faber explains large managers like BlackRock and Vanguard have not launched shareholder yield funds because they are in 'narrative jail' after 30 years of promoting dividend growth, so adoption would require an entirely new product rather than a strategy change.
insights.speaker: Meb Faber
insights.so_what: Explains why a demonstrably better strategy stays uncrowded 13 years after SYLD launched — an incumbent-inertia moat benefiting boutique sponsors.
insights.quote: they're in sort of a narrative jail where if they've been promoting dividend growth for 30 years, all of a sudden they say, just kidding, let's incorporate buybacks

insights.claim: Faber names three universal allocation mistakes — US-only exposure, market-cap weighting with no value or small/mid tilt, and zero real assets (commodities, commodity equities, TIPS, global REITs) — plus the absence of trend following as his fourth and most contrarian addition.
insights.speaker: Meb Faber
insights.so_what: A four-point audit an allocator can run against any retail, professional or institutional portfolio today; Faber notes TIPS look good now and REITs via BLDG are having a surprisingly strong year.

insights.claim: Faber allocates most of his own money to TRTY, Cambria's largest allocation ETF, which pairs roughly half buy-and-hold global allocation (GAA-style) with half trend following (GMOM-style) that can go 100% cash and bonds if markets roll over.
insights.speaker: Meb Faber
insights.so_what: Skin-in-the-game signal for the buy-and-hold plus trend barbell as the manager's preferred all-weather structure.
insights.quote: which is called Trinity, TRTY, uh which I think is our largest allocation ETF, and it's what I do with most of my money

insights.claim: Cambria's VAMO is currently 50% hedged with futures — its hedge ratio can range from zero to 100% — specifically because the broad market is expensive but still rising.
insights.speaker: Meb Faber
insights.so_what: A live positioning readout: the manager is running half-hedged equity exposure, the concrete expression of his yellow-light valuation view.
insights.quote: Currently, it's 50% hedged cuz the broad market's expensive but going up.

insights.claim: GVAL selects roughly the cheapest third of about 45 countries — 12 to 15 markets — using CAPE plus cash flow, dividends and book value, then buys the top 10 stocks from each market's top 30 by market cap and rebalances once a year.
insights.speaker: Meb Faber
insights.so_what: A top-down country-value process landing in high-single-digit to low-double-digit CAPE markets that produces very different holdings than bottom-up value screens.

themes.theme: Fixed Income Yield Gap and the Debt Trade

insights.claim: Faber calls insufficient yield in fixed income one of his hills to die on — relative to T-bills there is not enough spread compensation, so Cambria's value-based bond fund and its trend-based bond fund currently show little overlap.
insights.speaker: Meb Faber
insights.so_what: Argues for staying in T-bills rather than reaching into risky credit sleeves until spreads widen — and he says razor-thin corporate and junk spreads are the next tail-risk hedge Cambria may productize.
insights.quote: one of my hills to die on is there's not enough yield in fixed income

insights.claim: Faber believes rates could and should go higher and says this would surprise a lot of people, describing himself as a lone wolf on the view.
insights.speaker: Meb Faber
insights.so_what: A contrarian duration call against consensus expectations for lower rates; short duration and T-bills benefit if he is right.
insights.quote: it feels like uh rates could and should go higher, which I think would surprise a lot of people

insights.claim: On the national debt, Faber concludes all roads lead to inflation and that the correct response is asset ownership, noting US households are an order of magnitude more invested in equities than European households, which he frames as a structural advantage.
insights.speaker: Meb Faber
insights.so_what: Frames equity and real-asset ownership rather than any specific rates trade as the default hedge against fiscal deterioration.
insights.quote: all roads to me lead to inflation
